social.author: @dgar@aus.social
social.text: I've re-written this post four times, because I can't work out how to say the thing I want to say. I've given up and I'm just going to ramble until I think I'm done. While learning # Blender sometimes I'd get stuck with a particular aspect of the project I'm working on. When this happens, I’d look for some kind of guide or tutorial by searching for "(thing I'm having trouble with) Blender Tutorial". I found this sometimes limited my progress, because often the "thing I'm having trouble with" is actually unrelated to Blender entirely. With Blender you're often able to apply the skills and knowledge from disciplines you have learned in the real world. If you have some experience in Film or Television, then you have a head start in knowing how to frame a camera and properly light a scene. If you have experience in architecture, you might have a much easier time when designing a house or building in a Blender scene. If you have a background in animation, a lot of the animating tools will make sense to you. If you can code, then the nodes system might be easier for you than it is for me. So when you're stuck, try looking up a guide on the discipline without specifically looking for a "Blender Tutorial" on that subject. If you're struggling with animation, look up "How to Animate" or "The 12 Principles of Animation", because that base knowledge will transfer to the tools in Blender. The things that took me the most time when making my Space Pop music video, which was my first major Blender project, were sculpting a face, and styling hair. I have never done anything with sculpting or hairdressing, but the most helpful learning materials were the ones that were made by sculptors who make physical sculptures, and real-life hairdressers. I lost weeks trying to make hair that didn't look awful. Actually, that probably had more to do with the particle simulation system that my inexperience with hair-dressing, but they both played a part! Because once you have the hang of basic 3d modelling, you end up being drawn into these simulation systems. They promise to make things easier. Want a field of grass where every blade waves slightly in the breeze? Well, you can hand place each piece of grass in the field, and then animate each one by hand - or you can use a particle simulation to scatter the grass across the whole field in one step, and then simulate a breeze blowing them all. Well, simulations sound like a great idea!! Unfortunately, it's a whole new level of complexity with confusing attributes and settings, and if you get anything wrong, nothing works. What should have saved you time, ends up costing days of banging your head on a wall. Perhaps hand placement and individual animation of each blade wan't so bad after all... I recommend learning Blender. It's amazingly powerful, and completely free. Be warned though, it has a reputation for breaking people. If you can persevere though, it's totally worth it. BEYOND THE REHEARSAL; Series 2 The Heart Behind the Voice: Preparing the Singer, Not Just the Song “A choir may rehearse its songs for hours and still miss the most important preparation: preparing the hearts of the people who will sing them.”— Victor Adenola Introduction: Are We Preparing Voices or People? In Series One, we explored how a choir rehearsal can become more than a musical activity. We considered the possibility that a song rehearsed within the church could reach someone who is hurting, searching for hope, or silently struggling with life. But this raises another important question: If the message we sing is meant to touch lives, what kind of people are we becoming while preparing to deliver that message? A choir can have beautiful voices, excellent harmonies, and impressive musical arrangements. Yet, if its members lack understanding, humility, discipline, and genuine care for others, something important may be missing. The purpose of rehearsal is not simply to make the choir sound better. It is also an opportunity to develop the people behind the sound. The Message Must First Become Meaningful to the Messenger Imagine a singer leading a song about God’s faithfulness without considering what faithfulness means. Another sings about love without showing love to fellow choir members. Someone sings about forgiveness while holding tightly to bitterness. Does this mean such people cannot sing those songs? Not necessarily. We are all growing, learning, and working through personal challenges. However, it reminds us that singing a message and understanding its message are two different things. A singer should ask: What is this song communicating? What truth does it present? What response should it inspire? How can I communicate this message sincerely? We do not need to have perfect lives before we sing. But we must remain willing to grow in the truth we proclaim. Food for thought : Have you ever sung a song repeatedly without stopping to think about what its words actually mean? Your Character Is Part of Your Ministry A choir member’s ministry does not begin when the microphone is switched on, nor does it end when the service closes. It is reflected in how we speak to others, respond to correction, handle disagreements, honour commitments, and treat people who cannot offer us anything in return. A singer who performs beautifully but constantly humiliates fellow members creates a contradiction between the message being sung and the behaviour being displayed. This is not a call for perfection. It is a call for consistency. We should be willing to ask ourselves: Does the way I live support the message I communicate through music? A healthy choir therefore develops more than musical ability. It builds patience, respect, accountability, teamwork, and emotional maturity. -Victor Adenola Food for thought : If someone observed your behaviour during rehearsal without hearing you sing, would they still see the values your songs communicate? Understand the Person Behind the Voice One may be excited about a recent achievement. Another may be worried about school fees, family responsibilities, work, relationships, or an unanswered prayer. Someone else may be struggling quietly with discouragement. Yet, everyone is expected to sing together. This is why choir leadership requires more than musical knowledge. It requires awareness of people. A choir leader should not assume that every mistake is caused by laziness, every silence is disrespect, or every absence means a lack of commitment. Sometimes correction is necessary; sometimes a conversation is needed first. -Victor Adenola This does not mean standards should be abandoned. Rather, correction should be firm without being cruel, and discipline should leave room for understanding. A choir can maintain excellence while treating its members with dignity. “A choir is not just a collection of voices. It is a community of people, each carrying a story that may never be heard from the microphone.”— Victor Adenola Food for thought : Do we pay attention only to what choir members contribute, or do we also care about the people making those contributions? Rehearsal Is Also a School of Relationships Choir rehearsals bring together people with different personalities, abilities, experiences, and expectations. Some learn quickly; others need more time. Some are confident; others are afraid of making mistakes. Some naturally take initiative, while others need encouragement. These differences can become sources of conflict—or opportunities for growth. A healthy choir learns to listen to one another, accept correction, share responsibility, and celebrate improvement. Members should be able to make mistakes during learning without becoming objects of ridicule. Musical excellence is difficult to sustain in an atmosphere of fear, hostility, and unhealthy competition. _ Victor Adenola When members feel respected, they are more likely to ask questions, acknowledge weaknesses, and contribute meaningfully. The goal is not to remove every disagreement. It is to learn how to handle disagreements without destroying unity. “Unity is not the absence of differences. It is the discipline of bringing our differences under a shared purpose.”— Victor Adenola Food for thought : Is your rehearsal room a place where people become more confident and capable, or a place where they become afraid to make mistakes? Sing With Understanding, Not Just Emotion Emotion has a place in gospel music. A song about gratitude may inspire joy; a song about repentance may encourage reflection; a song about hope may bring comfort. But emotion alone cannot replace understanding and technicality. A singer may feel deeply moved by a song and still communicate its message poorly. Another may sing with restraint yet communicate the words with remarkable clarity. The question is not simply, “How do I feel while singing this song?” It is also, “What should the listener understand from it?” Before rehearsing a song, consider these three questions: What is the message? Understand the words and the truth they communicate. What is the mood? Identify the emotion that supports the message without exaggerating it. What is the purpose? Determine why the song is being presented at that particular time. These questions help singers make better musical decisions. They influence phrasing, dynamics, tempo, articulation, and the way the choir communicates together. “Emotion can add colour to a song, but understanding gives that colour direction.”— Victor Adenola Food for thought : Are you singing because you understand what the song communicates, or because you have become familiar with how it sounds? A Choir Should Be a Safe Place to Grow A choir should challenge people to improve, but it should not make them feel worthless when they are still learning. There is a difference between correcting a mistake and attacking a person. Compare these two statements: “You are not good enough to sing this part.” “This part needs more work. Let us practise it slowly until you can sing it confidently.” Both acknowledge a problem, but only the second provides a clear path towards improvement. The same principle applies to leadership. Leaders should set expectations, provide direction, and hold members accountable without using shame as their primary method of correction. Members also have a responsibility to receive feedback with humility and a willingness to improve. A safe environment is not one without standards. It is one where people can pursue high standards without being stripped of their dignity. _Victor Adenola “Correction should reveal the path to improvement, not convince a person that improvement is impossible.”— Victor Adenola Food for thought : When you correct someone, do your words make improvement seem possible—or make the person feel that they have no value? The Unseen Listener Is Still Important Remember the man whose story inspired this series: a person who was contemplating suicide, heard a choir rehearsing, followed the sound to the church, and sat at the back crying before a minister attended to him. However, the lesson is not that music alone can resolve every crisis. Rather, music can become a point of connection—a reason for someone to enter a place where compassion, conversation, prayer, and appropriate support may become possible. We cannot predict every impact of a song. We can, however, prepare responsibly and remain attentive to the people around us. “We may never know who will hear our song, but we can decide how faithfully we prepare to serve whoever is listening.”— Victor Adenola Practical Steps: Preparing the Heart Before the Song The next time your choir gathers for rehearsal, try these simple practices: Before rehearsal Read and understand the lyrics. Reflect on the message of the song. Arrive prepared and ready to learn. Set aside unnecessary distractions. During rehearsal Listen to the director and fellow singers. Accept correction without hostility. Encourage members who are struggling. Focus on communicating the message, not competing for attention. After rehearsal Reflect on what you have learnt. Identify one area where you need to improve. Address misunderstandings respectfully. Consider how your attitude and conduct can better support the choir’s purpose. These practices may appear simple, but consistent habits shape the culture of a choir over time. Conclusion: Let the Preparation Change You A meaningful choir rehearsal should produce more than a polished song. It should contribute to the growth of the people singing it. As we develop our voices, let us also develop our understanding. As we pursue musical excellence, let us practise humility. As we communicate messages of love and hope, let us become more attentive to the people around us. We may not always see the outcome of our service. Some listeners may never tell us what a song meant to them. Some of our most important contributions may happen beyond the spotlight. But that should not make our preparation less intentional. It should make it more meaningful. “The true value of a choir is not measured only by the beauty of its sound, but also by the understanding, discipline, and compassion that shape the people behind it.” — Victor Adenola Coming Next — Series Three: Beyond the Rehearsal: Building a Choir That Serves With Purpose #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #culture #genre #gospel #gospelmusic #ImprovedDisciplineAndPatience #musicDirector #Musicalmind #musicians #musicperformance #Purpose #rehearsals #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers
